claim: The Arabidopsis active demethylase ROS1 promotes basal resistance towards Pseudomonas syringae by antagonizing RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM).
source: Here, we first show that the Arabidopsis active demethylase ROS1 promotes basal resistance towards Pseudomonas syringae by antagonizing RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing enhanced susceptibility in ros1 mutants and rescue in ros1dcl23 mutants (Figure 1)

claim: ROS1 facilitates the flagellin-triggered induction of the disease resistance gene RMG1 by limiting RdDM at the 3' boundary of a transposable element (TE)-derived repeat embedded in its promoter.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that ROS1 facilitates the flagellin-triggered induction of the disease resistance gene RMG1 by limiting RdDM at the 3' boundary of a transposable element (TE)-derived repeat embedded in its promoter.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing compromised RMG1 induction in ros1 mutants and restoration in ros1dcl23 mutants (Figure 2)

claim: At a subset of promoters, ROS1 erases methylation at discrete regions exhibiting WRKY transcription factors (TFs) binding.
source: We further identify flagellin-responsive ROS1 putative primary targets and show that at a subset of promoters, ROS1 erases methylation at discrete regions exhibiting WRKY transcription factors (TFs) binding.
evidence: Supported by GAT analysis showing WRKY TF binding enrichment at demethylated promoter regions (Figure 4)

claim: ROS1 removes methylation at the orphan immune receptor RLP43 promoter to ensure DNA binding of WRKY TFs.
source: In particular, we demonstrate that ROS1 removes methylation at the orphan immune receptor RLP43 promoter, to ensure DNA binding of WRKY TFs.
evidence: Supported by DAP-qPCR experiments showing abolished WRKY binding to methylated RLP43 promoter in ros1 mutants (Figure 5)

claim: ROS1-directed demethylation of RMG1 and RLP43 promoters is causal for both flagellin responsiveness of these genes and for basal resistance.
source: Finally, we show that ROS1-directed demethylation of RMG1 and RLP43 promoters is causal for both flagellin responsiveness of these genes and for basal resistance.
evidence: Supported by experiments with IR-RMG1p/RLP43p transgenic lines showing compromised gene induction and enhanced susceptibility (Figure 6)

claim: ros1-3 and ros1-4 mutant leaves exhibited enhanced spreading of Pto DC3000 in Arabidopsis leaf secondary veins.
source: We have previously reported that ros1 mutants exhibit enhanced spreading of Pto DC3000 in Arabidopsis leaf secondary veins (Yu et al., 2013). This phenotype was further confirmed here when ros1-3 and ros1-4 mutant leaves were wound-inoculated with a GFP-tagged Pto DC3000 (Pto DC3000-GFP) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from wound-inoculation assays and previous publication

claim: An enhanced bacterial titre was observed in ros1-3 and ros1-4 alleles dip-inoculated with Pto DC3000-GFP.
source: In addition, an enhanced bacterial titre was observed in these ros1 alleles dip-inoculated with Pto DC3000-GFP (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data presented in Figure 1C

claim: ROS1 positively regulates basal resistance against Pto DC3000.
source: These data indicate that ROS1 positively regulates basal resistance against Pto DC3000.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced susceptibility phenotypes in ros1 mutants

claim: ROS1 antagonizes methylation at thousands of loci, which are methylated in a RdDM-dependent or -independent manner.
source: It has been shown that ROS1 antagonizes methylation at thousands of loci, which are methylated in a RdDM-dependent or -independent manner (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication

claim: Both the enhanced vascular propagation and apoplastic growth of Pto DC3000-GFP detected in the ros1-3 mutant were reduced in ros1dcl23 mutants, and almost comparable to the phenotypes of Col-0-infected plants.
source: Interestingly, we found that both the enhanced vascular propagation and apoplastic growth of Pto DC3000-GFP detected in the ros1-3 mutant were reduced in ros1dcl23 mutants, and almost comparable to the phenotypes of Col-0-infected plants (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from infection assays in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: DCL2 and/or DCL3 are mainly responsible for the enhanced susceptible phenotypes observed in ros1-3-infected mutants.
source: These data indicate that DCL2 and/or DCL3 are mainly responsible for the enhanced susceptible phenotypes observed in ros1-3-infected mutants.
evidence: Inferred from rescue of susceptibility phenotype in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: Some defence genes are likely hypermethylated and silenced in the ros1-3 mutants through the action of, at least in part, DCL2- and/or DCL3-dependent siRNAs.
source: They also suggest that some defence genes are likely hypermethylated and silenced in the ros1-3 mutants through the action of, at least in part, DCL2- and/or DCL3-dependent siRNAs.
evidence: Speculative inference based on genetic rescue experiments

claim: ROS1 has previously been shown to ensure a proper flg22-triggered induction of RMG1, an orphan TNL that is demethylated by ROS1 in its promoter.
source: ROS1 has previously been shown to ensure a proper flg22-triggered induction of RMG1, an orphan TNL that is demethylated by ROS1 in its promoter (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication

claim: A strong reduction in flg22-mediated inducibility of RMG1 is observed in the absence of ROS1.
source: As a result, a strong reduction in flg22-mediated inducibility of RMG1 is observed in the absence of ROS1 (Figure 2D and F; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and previous publication

claim: Both rmg1-1 and rmg1-2 mutants lack RMG1 mRNA in leaves treated with flg22 compared to Col-0.
source: To investigate the possible contribution of RMG1 in basal resistance against Pto DC3000, we have isolated and characterized two independent T-DNA insertion lines, which lack RMG1 mRNA in leaves treated with flg22 compared to Col-0 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing absence of RMG1 mRNA

claim: Both rmg1-1 and rmg1-2 mutants exhibited elevated bacterial vascular propagation and apoplastic growth compared to Col-0-infected plants.
source: Both mutants exhibited elevated bacterial vascular propagation and apoplastic growth compared to Col-0-infected plants (Figure 2B and C)
evidence: Supported by bacterial infection assay data

claim: RMG1 is a functional disease resistance gene that contributes to basal resistance towards Pto DC3000.
source: indicating that RMG1 is a functional disease resistance gene that contributes to basal resistance towards Pto DC3000.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced susceptibility in rmg1 mutants

claim: The heightened susceptibility of the ros1-infected mutants might be in part attributed to the silencing of RMG1.
source: These data also suggest that the heightened susceptibility of the ros1-infected mutants might be in part attributed to the silencing of RMG1.
evidence: Speculative inference based on RMG1 function and its regulation by ROS1

claim: RMG1 contains two remnant RC/Helitron TEs in its promoter: the distal repeat AtREP4 (At4TE29275) and the proximal repeat AtREP11 (At4TE29280).
source: RMG1 contains two remnant RC/Helitron TEs in its promoter: the distal repeat AtREP4 (At4TE29275) and the proximal repeat AtREP11 (At4TE29280) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by genomic annotation and visualization in Figure 2D

claim: AtREP4 is targeted by 23–24 nt siRNAs and methylated in the Arabidopsis reference accession Col-0.
source: AtREP4 is targeted by 23–24 nt siRNAs and methylated in the Arabidopsis reference accession Col-0, a regulatory process that presumably maintains a low basal expression of this gene in untreated conditions (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by previous publication and current data

claim: AtREP11 is unmethylated in Col-0 but hypermethylated in a ros1 mutant.
source: By contrast, AtREP11 (At4TE29280), which is located 216 bp upstream of RMG1 start codon, is unmethylated in Col-0 but hypermethylated in a ros1 mutant, as previously demonstrated by a targeted bisulfite Sanger sequencing approach (Yu et al., 2013). These results were confirmed by using a whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (BS-seq) approach in rosette leaves of untreated Col-0 and ros1-3 mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by BS-seq data and previous publication

claim: The hyper differentially methylated region (hyperDMR) detected at the AtREP11 repeat was particularly pronounced at the 3' boundary of this remnant RC/Helitron TE in the ros1-3 mutant, while this region was unmethylated in Col-0 plants.
source: We found that the hyper differentially methylated region (hyperDMR) detected at the AtREP11 repeat was particularly pronounced at the 3' boundary of this remnant RC/Helitron TE in the ros1-3 mutant, while this region was unmethylated in Col-0 plants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by BS-seq data shown in Figure 2D

claim: ROS1 limits the spreading of DNA methylation at TE boundaries.
source: This result is consistent with a role of ROS1 in limiting the spreading of DNA methylation at TE boundaries (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication and current observations

claim: While no siRNA was retrieved at the 3' boundary of AtREP11 in Col-0 plants, siRNA species of different sizes were detected in the ros1-3 mutant, ranging from low levels in the 21–22 nt species to high levels in the 23–24 nt species.
source: While no siRNA was retrieved at the 3' boundary of AtREP11 in Col-0 plants, we detected the accumulation of siRNA species of different sizes in the ros1-3 mutant, ranging from low levels in the 21–22 nt species to high levels in the 23–24 nt species (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by sRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: All siRNAs at the 3' boundary of AtREP11 were no longer produced in ros1dcl23 mutants, a molecular effect which was associated with an absence of cytosine methylation at this ROS1-targeted region.
source: All these siRNAs were no longer produced in ros1dcl23 mutants, a molecular effect which was associated with an absence of cytosine methylation at this ROS1-targeted region (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by sRNA-seq and BS-seq data in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: DCL2- and/or DCL3-dependent siRNAs direct RdDM predominantly at the 3' boundary of AtREP11 in the ros1-3 mutant.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that DCL2- and/or DCL3-dependent siRNAs direct RdDM predominantly at the 3' boundary of AtREP11 in the ros1-3 mutant.
evidence: Inferred from loss of siRNAs and methylation in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: In Col-0 plants, ROS1 counteracts the biogenesis of DCL2- and DCL3-dependent siRNAs at the RMG1 promoter region to restrict DNA methylation spreading at the 3' boundary of AtREP11.
source: They also suggest that, in Col-0 plants, ROS1 counteracts the biogenesis of DCL2- and DCL3-dependent siRNAs at this RMG1 promoter region to restrict DNA methylation spreading at the 3' boundary of AtREP11.
evidence: Speculative inference based on genetic and molecular data

claim: A compromised induction of RMG1 was observed in the ros1-3-elicited mutant that was not observed for FRK1.
source: We found a compromised induction of RMG1 in the ros1-3-elicited mutant that was not observed for Flg22-induced Receptor-like Kinase 1 (FRK1), which is not hypermethylated in ros1-3 mutants, and thus served as a control (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data and BS-seq data showing no hypermethylation at FRK1

claim: A full restoration of flg22-triggered inducibility of RMG1 was observed in the ros1dcl23-elicited mutant.
source: By contrast, a full restoration of flg22-triggered inducibility of RMG1 was observed in the ros1dcl23-elicited mutant (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: RdDM of AtREP11 and its 3' boundary, which is specifically detected in ros1-3 mutants, negatively regulates the flg22 inducibility of RMG1.
source: These data indicate that RdDM of AtREP11 and its 3' boundary, which is specifically detected in ros1-3 mutants, negatively regulates the flg22 inducibility of RMG1.
evidence: Inferred from restoration of RMG1 induction in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: ROS1-directed demethylation of the RMG1 promoter region is crucial to ensure a proper transcriptional activation of this gene during flg22 elicitation.
source: They also suggest that ROS1-directed demethylation of this RMG1 promoter region is crucial to ensure a proper transcriptional activation of this gene during flg22 elicitation.
evidence: Speculative inference based on genetic and molecular data

claim: 2076 differentially expressed genes were identified, among which, 907 were less-induced and 1169 less-repressed in flg22-treated ros1-3 mutants compared to Col-0.
source: Using this approach, we identified 2076 differentially expressed genes, among which, 907 were less-induced and 1169 less-repressed in flg22-treated ros1-3 mutants compared to Col-0 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: 217 candidate genes were recovered representing ~10% of the whole flg22-responsive and ROS1 regulated genes, among them, 102 less-induced and 115 less-repressed genes.
source: As a result of this analysis, 217 candidate genes were recovered, representing ~10% of the whole flg22-responsive and ROS1 regulated genes. Among them, 102 less-induced (promoter regions: 44 DMRs; gene bodies: 33; downstream regions: 25) and 115 less-repressed (promoter regions: 67 DMRs; gene bodies: 27; downstream regions: 21) genes were recovered (Figure 3A, Supplementary File 1).
evidence: Supported by integrated analysis of RNA-seq and BS-seq data

claim: The overall increase of methylation levels at the 102 less-induced genes and at the whole 2943 ROS1 targets, in ros1-3 compared to Col-0 plants, was almost exclusively observed in 2 Kb upstream sequence regions.
source: We found that the overall increase of methylation levels at the 102 less-induced genes and at the whole 2943 ROS1 targets, in ros1-3 compared to Col-0 plants, was almost exclusively observed in 2 Kb upstream sequence regions (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by BS-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: An increase in siRNA accumulation was detected at both the promoters of the flg22-induced and overall ROS1 targets in ros1-3 versus Col-0 plants.
source: An increase in siRNA accumulation was also detected at both the promoters of the flg22-induced and overall ROS1 targets in ros1-3 versus Col-0 plants (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sRNA-seq data analysis

claim: The overall enhanced DNA methylation and siRNA levels observed in ros1-3 mutants at these loci were almost restored to Col-0 levels in ros1dcl23 mutants.
source: By contrast, the overall enhanced DNA methylation and siRNA levels observed in ros1-3 mutants at these loci were almost restored to Col-0 levels in ros1dcl23 mutants (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by BS-seq and sRNA-seq data in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: ROS1 directs promoter demethylation mostly by antagonizing DCL2 and/or DCL3 functions.
source: The latter data suggest that ROS1 directs promoter demethylation mostly by antagonizing DCL2 and/or DCL3 functions.
evidence: Inferred from restoration of methylation and siRNA levels in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: The expression pattern of the phosphoglycerate mutase gene was similar to the one of RMG1: the compromised flg22 induction of this gene was almost fully rescued in elicited ros1dcl23 mutants.
source: The expression pattern of the phosphoglycerate mutase gene was similar to the one of RMG1: the compromised flg22 induction of this gene was almost fully rescued in elicited ros1dcl23 mutants, which is consistent with a loss of siRNAs and DNA methylation at its hyperDMR in untreated ros1dcl23 mutants (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR, BS-seq, and sRNA-seq data

claim: The flg22-triggered induction of RBA1 was restored in ros1dcl23 to levels similar to dcl23 mutants, but not to the same extent as in elicited Col-0 plants.
source: The flg22-triggered induction of RBA1 was restored in ros1dcl23 to levels similar to dcl23 mutants, but not to the same extent as in elicited Col-0 plants (Figure 3G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data

claim: This effect was associated with a partial decrease in RBA1 promoter methylation at the RBA1 hyperDMR, in ros1dcl23 compared to ros1-3 mutants.
source: Furthermore, this effect was associated with a partial decrease in RBA1 promoter methylation at the RBA1 hyperDMR, in ros1dcl23 compared to ros1-3 mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by BS-seq data

claim: RLP43 remained fully silenced in the ros1dcl23-treated mutants, as in elicited ros1-3 mutants, which is consistent with comparable levels of RLP43 promoter methylation in both untreated mutants.
source: By contrast, RLP43 remained fully silenced in the ros1dcl23-treated mutants, as in elicited ros1-3 mutants, which is consistent with comparable levels of RLP43 promoter methylation in both untreated mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 3E, Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and BS-seq data

claim: The unaltered RLP43 hyperDMR detected in the ros1dcl23 mutants was associated with a moderate remaining accumulation of siRNAs, which was shifted from 23 to 24 nt siRNAs in ros1-3 to 21 nt siRNAs in ros1dcl23 mutants.
source: It is noteworthy that the unaltered RLP43 hyperDMR detected in the ros1dcl23 mutants was associated with a moderate remaining accumulation of siRNAs, which was shifted from 23 to 24 nt siRNAs in ros1-3 to 21 nt siRNAs in ros1dcl23 mutants (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by sRNA-seq data

claim: The unaltered RLP43 hyperDMR was accompanied by the presence of longer RNAs (25–29 nt), which exhibit a preference for having an A at their 5' ends and that overlap with siRNAs produced from the hyperDMR, as observed for typical P4RNA species.
source: It was also accompanied by the presence of longer RNAs (25–29 nt), which exhibit a preference for having an A at their 5' ends and that overlap with siRNAs produced from the hyperDMR, as observed for typical P4RNA species (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Blevins et al., 2015; Zhai et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by sRNA-seq data and citations to previous publications

claim: PolIV-dependent 21 nt siRNAs and P4RNAs are competent for RdDM.
source: Because PolIV-dependent 21 nt siRNAs and P4RNAs are competent for RdDM (Yang et al., 2016; Panda et al., 2020), the above RNA entities might maintain RdDM at RLP43 promoter in the ros1dcl23 mutants, although RNA-independent mechanism(s) might additionally contribute to this process.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications and speculative inference

claim: The flg22-triggered induction of the phosphoglycerate mutase, RBA1, and RLP43 genes is facilitated by ROS1, which prevents hypermethylation at discrete regions in their promoters.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the flg22-triggered induction of these three genes is facilitated by ROS1, which prevents hypermethylation at discrete regions in their promoters.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and molecular data across multiple genes

claim: The promoter hypermethylation of the phosphoglycerate mutase, RBA1, and RLP43 genes detected in ros1-3 mutants can be fully or partially altered upon concomitant removal of DCL2 and DCL3, or unchanged.
source: They also indicate that their promoter hypermethylation detected in ros1-3 mutants can be fully or partially altered upon concomitant removal of DCL2 and DCL3, as found at the phosphoglycerate mutase and RBA1 genes, respectively, or unchanged, as observed at the RLP43 locus.
evidence: Inferred from differential responses in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: 14 out of 26 promoter-derived sequences tested exhibited in vitro DNA binding of WRKY TFs.
source: By using this analysis, we found in vitro DNA binding of WRKY TFs at 14 out of 26 promoter-derived sequences tested (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by GAT analysis of DAP-seq data

claim: Only 2 out of 28 less-repressed stringent targets displayed WRKY TFs enrichment at their demethylated promoter regions.
source: By contrast, only 2 out of 28 less-repressed stringent targets displayed WRKY TFs enrichment at their demethylated promoter regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GAT analysis of DAP-seq data

claim: RMG1, RBA1, and RLP43 exhibit in vitro DNA binding of several WRKYs in their promoter regions subjected to ROS1-directed demethylation.
source: Among the 14 less-induced candidates, we retrieved RMG1, RBA1, and RLP43, which exhibit in vitro DNA binding of several WRKYs in their promoter regions subjected to ROS1-directed demethylation (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by GAT analysis and DAP-seq data

claim: Five out of 14 candidate promoters exhibit in vivo binding of the AtWRKY18 and AtWRKY40 based on ChIP-seq data sets generated in flg22-challenged transgenic seedlings.
source: Five out of these 14 candidate promoters also exhibit in vivo binding of the AtWRKY18 and AtWRKY40 based on chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data sets generated in flg22-challenged transgenic seedlings (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; Birkenbihl et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data from previous publication

claim: The chromatin association of PAMP-responsive WRKYs was specifically detected during flg22 treatment, indicating that PTI signalling is required for this chromatin-based regulatory process.
source: Importantly, the chromatin association of these PAMP-responsive WRKYs was specifically detected during flg22 treatment, indicating that PTI signalling is required for this chromatin-based regulatory process (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data showing flg22-dependent WRKY binding

claim: The in vivo binding of AtWRKY40 at the RLP43 promoter specifically occurs during flg22 elicitation and at the demethylated promoter region, which contains a single W-box cis-regulatory element.
source: For example, the in vivo binding of AtWRKY40 at the RLP43 promoter specifically occurs during flg22 elicitation and at the demethylated promoter region, which contains a single W-box cis-regulatory element (Figure 4B and C; Birkenbihl et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data and genomic sequence analysis

claim: A strong reduction in GUS staining and mRNA levels was found in flg22-challenged leaves of primary transformants expressing the W-box mutant- versus the WT-versions of the RLP43 transcriptional reporters.
source: We found a strong reduction in GUS staining and mRNA levels in flg22-challenged leaves of primary transformants expressing the W-box mutant- versus the WT-versions of the RLP43 transcriptional reporters (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by GUS staining and RT-qPCR data from transgenic plants

claim: The W-box cis-element at the RLP43 promoter is functional and essential for the flg22-triggered transcriptional activation of RLP43.
source: These results imply that this W-box cis-element is functional and essential for the flg22-triggered transcriptional activation of RLP43.
evidence: Inferred from reduced GUS expression in W-box mutant reporter lines

claim: The remaining GUS staining detected in the leaf vasculature of flg22-treated plants expressing the W-box mutant transgene suggests that other TFs must additionally contribute to the flg22-triggered transcriptional activation of RLP43 in these tissues.
source: Nevertheless, the remaining GUS staining detected in the leaf vasculature of flg22-treated plants expressing the W-box mutant transgene suggests that other TFs must additionally contribute to the flg22-triggered transcriptional activation of RLP43 in these tissues (Figure 4F).
evidence: Speculative inference based on residual GUS activity in W-box mutant

claim: The W-box cis-element located in the demethylated region of the RLP43 promoter is the site for WRKY TF binding.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the W-box cis-element located in the demethylated region of the RLP43 promoter is the site for WRKY TF binding.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including DAP-seq, ChIP-seq, and functional reporter assays

claim: The flg22-triggered recruitment of WRKYs at the RLP43 promoter is critical for the transcriptional activation of this gene during PTI.
source: They also suggest that the flg22-triggered recruitment of WRKYs at the RLP43 promoter is critical for the transcriptional activation of this gene during PTI.
evidence: Speculative inference based on W-box mutant reporter data

claim: DNA methylation has previously been shown to inhibit, in some instances, TF-DNA binding.
source: DNA methylation has previously been shown to inhibit, in some instances, TF-DNA binding (Watt and Molloy, 1988; Iguchi-Ariga and Schaffner, 1989; Tate and Bird, 1993; O'Malley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications

claim: A DAP-seq study performed with Col-0 genomic DNA revealed that ~75% of Arabidopsis TFs are sensitive to DNA methylation.
source: For example, a DAP-seq study performed with Col-0 genomic DNA revealed that ~75% of Arabidopsis TFs are sensitive to DNA methylation (O'Malley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication

claim: Several WRKY TFs are sensitive to DNA methylation.
source: This was notably the case of several WRKY TFs used in their analysis (Figure 5A; O'Malley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by DAP-seq data from previous publication

claim: Both AtWRKY18 and AtWRKY40 exhibit strong and comparable enrichment at the RLP43 and bZIP60 promoters in the presence of Col-0 genomic DNA.
source: Using this DAP-qPCR approach, we found that both WRKY TFs exhibit strong and comparable enrichment at the RLP43 and bZIP60 promoters in the presence of Col-0 genomic DNA (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by DAP-qPCR experimental data

claim: No WRKY binding was found at RLP43 and bZIP60 promoters with GST alone.
source: while no binding was found with GST alone (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by DAP-qPCR control experiments

claim: The DNA binding of AtWRKY18 and AtWRKY40 was almost fully abolished at the RLP43 promoter with genomic DNA from ros1-3 mutants, while it remained unaltered at the bZIP60 promoter in the same conditions.
source: By contrast, the DNA binding of these Arabidopsis WRKY TFs was almost fully abolished at the RLP43 promoter with genomic DNA from ros1-3 mutants, while it remained unaltered at the bZIP60 promoter in the same conditions (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by DAP-qPCR experimental data

claim: The hypermethylation observed in ros1-3 mutants at the RLP43 promoter directly repels DNA binding of WRKY TFs.
source: Collectively, these data provide evidence that the hypermethylation observed in ros1-3 mutants at the RLP43 promoter directly repels DNA binding of WRKY TFs.
evidence: Inferred from DAP-qPCR data showing loss of WRKY binding to methylated DNA

claim: Molecular characterization by northern blot and McrBC-qPCR analyses revealed levels of siRNA accumulation and of methylation at RMG1 and RLP43 promoter regions that were comparable to the ones detected in ros1-3 mutants.
source: Molecular characterization by northern blot and McrBC-qPCR analyses, respectively, revealed levels of siRNA accumulation and of methylation at these promoter regions that were comparable to the ones detected in ros1-3 mutants (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by northern blot and McrBC-qPCR data from IR transgenic lines

claim: The induction of RMG1 and RLP43 was strongly altered in the two IR-RMG1p/RLP43p independent transgenic lines, almost to the same extent as in the ros1-elicited mutant background.
source: Significantly, we found that the induction of these genes was strongly altered in the two IR-RMG1p/RLP43p independent transgenic lines, almost to the same extent as in the ros1-elicited mutant background (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from IR transgenic lines

claim: The flg22-triggered induction of RBA1 and FRK1 was comparable in Col-0 and IR-RMG1p/RLP43p transgenic lines.
source: By contrast, the flg22-triggered induction of RBA1 and FRK1 was comparable in Col-0 and IR-RMG1p/RLP43p transgenic lines (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), supporting a specific transcriptional silencing effect towards RMG1 and RLP43.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing no effect on control genes

claim: IR-RMG1p/RLP43p lines displayed enhanced Pto DC3000 titres compared to Col-0-infected plants.
source: In addition, we found that IR-RMG1p/RLP43p lines displayed enhanced Pto DC3000 titres compared to Col-0-infected plants (Figure 6E), a phenotype resembling the one observed in rmg1-infected plants (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data

claim: Hypermethylation of RMG1 and RLP43 discrete promoter regions is causal for the compromised flg22 induction of these genes and for increased susceptibility towards Pto DC3000.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that hypermethylation of these RMG1 and RLP43 discrete promoter regions is causal for the compromised flg22 induction of these genes and for increased susceptibility towards Pto DC3000.
evidence: Inferred from IR transgenic line phenotypes

claim: ROS1-directed demethylation of RMG1 and RLP43 promoter regulatory sequences is critical for both flg22-triggered gene inducibility and antibacterial resistance.
source: We conclude that ROS1-directed demethylation of these promoter regulatory sequences is critical for both flg22-triggered gene inducibility and antibacterial resistance.
evidence: Inferred from comprehensive genetic and molecular data

claim: Arabidopsis ros1 mutants exhibited enhanced growth and vascular propagation of Pto DC3000, two phenotypes which were almost fully rescued in ros1dcl23-infected mutants.
source: Here, we showed that Arabidopsis ros1 mutants exhibited enhanced growth and vascular propagation of Pto DC3000, two phenotypes which were almost fully rescued in ros1dcl23-infected mutants (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by bacterial infection assay data

claim: ROS1 promotes basal resistance against Pto DC3000 mainly by antagonizing DCL2 and/or DCL3 functions.
source: Therefore, ROS1 promotes basal resistance against Pto DC3000 mainly by antagonizing DCL2 and/or DCL3 functions.
evidence: Inferred from genetic rescue experiments in ros1dcl23 mutants

claim: The reprogramming of more than 2000 genes was altered in ros1-elicited mutants, supporting a major role for ROS1 in controlling PAMP-triggered gene expression changes.
source: We further found that the reprogramming of more than 2000 genes was altered in ros1-elicited mutants, supporting a major role for ROS1 in controlling PAMP-triggered gene expression changes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Among flg22-responsive ROS1-regulated genes, only ~10% exhibited hyperDMRs in ros1 mutants and were thus potentially directly regulated by ROS1.
source: Among these genes, only ~10% exhibited hyperDMRs in ros1 mutants and were thus potentially directly regulated by ROS1.
evidence: Supported by integrated RNA-seq and BS-seq data analysis

claim: The majority of biotic stress-responsive genes are ROS1 secondary targets.
source: This is congruent with a previous transcriptome study conducted in ros1 mutants infected with Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (López Sánchez et al., 2016) and suggests that the majority of biotic stress-responsive genes are ROS1 secondary targets.
evidence: Inferred from proportion of direct vs indirect targets and supported by citation
